findings.symptom: A ToolDefinition array exported from a module under mcp-server/src/tools/ but never concatenated into index.ts's registry is served by nothing, advertised by nothing, and reported by no check: the tool-inventory gate stays green and DEVELOPMENT.md simply omits it.
findings.root_cause: gen-tool-inventory.mjs derives its denominator from the served tools/list. scanToolFiles() reads every src/tools/*.ts and does hold the full exported set, but that map is consulted only to group and order the served tools; its keys are never diffed against the served list, so the one artifact that sees both sides discards the only comparison that could turn red. check-tool-schemas.mjs imports every dist/tools module and therefore also sees an unregistered one, but asserts schema shape only.
findings.business_context: This is the subsystem's own recorded seam contract SM-03 — "a module whose array is not concatenated here is invisible with no error" — read back as a gate property. The repair is small and local: diff scanToolFiles()'s mapping keys against the served names and fail on either difference, which turns an unregistered module red and also catches an inventory entry the server no longer serves. Until then the registry is the one place in this server where an omission costs nothing.

dispositions.rationale: Containment here is structural rather than a prefix test — every existing segment is rejected if it is a symlink, is a non-directory before the leaf, or realpaths outside the root, and equality with the root is refused — and a tool-supplied output directory is resolved against storagePath before it reaches that check, which is why materialize_docs writes .amanuensis/docs and cannot be aimed at the repository root.

B-02 creates the two derived views by applying schema.sql and then asserts their presence by name, closing the connection and refusing the open if either is absent; it selects from neither and reimplements neither, so this subsystem holds no second copy of a view's predicate.
dispositions.overturn_argument: B-02 creates the two derived views by applying schema.sql and then asserts their presence by name, closing the connection and refusing the open if either is absent; it selects from neither and reimplements neither, so this subsystem holds no second copy of a view's predicate.

dispositions.rationale: B-02 records no revision of its own, and supplies the thing the phrase "resolves in the bound workspace" refers to: every revision probe in the server runs git with cwd set to project.workspacePath, a canonical root that is containment-asserted and receipt-bound rather than whatever directory the process was started in.

This subsystem carries the party the four-party contract cannot check statically — an existing database whose CHECK literals predate a widening, which CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS will never rewrite — and repairs it on every open by comparing the live DDL text against the source and rebuilding the table transactionally when the live one is strictly narrower.

Both halves of the concern are answered by code: a commit against the storage directory truncate-checkpoints the WAL first and raises rather than committing when the checkpoint is partial, so the committed memory.db is a recoverable file, and every git invocation is scoped to the storage directory by an explicit pathspec so a concurrent survey sharing one outer repository cannot be entangled into it.

The two assertions this subsystem makes are triggered by absence rather than satisfied by it: requireViews refuses the open precisely when a view is missing, and the WAL checkpoint raises on a busy or partial result instead of committing. The one silent path is migrateVocabularyChecks declining a table whose canonical CREATE it cannot locate in schema.sql, which is a contract error CI's --check-sql reads schema.sql to catch; it is recorded as a field note rather than passed over.

claim_targets.challenge: adversarial probe for claim B-02/concurrency did not overturn it: the probe looked for a lock that would make the claim's "not provided by this subsystem" wrong and found the write_locks table to be an advisory artifact-path registry tools opt into, never consulted by openDatabase or by any storage write, so nothing here detects a second writer.

adversarial probe for claim B-02/flow/storage-write/01 did not overturn it: resolveStorageOutputPath resolves a relative argument against project.storagePath and hands the result to assertContainedPath with storagePath as the root, so no argument — absolute, traversing, or symlinked — reaches a path outside the storage directory.

adversarial probe for claim B-02/key-type/mcp-server-src-project-ts-assertcontainedpath did not overturn it: the probe looked for the usual escape — a prefix comparison that a sibling directory sharing a name prefix would satisfy — and found isWithin plus a per-segment lstat and realpath walk, with equality to the root itself also refused.

adversarial probe for claim B-02/key-type/mcp-server-src-project-ts-projectcontext did not overturn it: ProjectContext's members are declared readonly and the binding receipt is built once in resolveProject; no tool handler writes back through the context, so a later call cannot rebind the workspace.

adversarial probe for claim B-02/state-container/mcp-server-src-db-ts-opendatabase did not overturn it: openDatabase is the only `new Database(...)` in the server; it sets WAL and foreign_keys, runs migrations strictly before initializeSchema, and closes the connection before throwing when a required view is absent — so a caller never receives a handle to a store that failed the view assertion.

dispositions.rationale: The schema does the half of boundary validation a substrate can do — a CHECK on every vocabulary-constrained column, so an out-of-enum value is refused by SQLite whatever the handler believed — and none of the half it cannot: containment of a path against a canonical root is not expressible in SQL and is asserted at ingress in B-02 and B-04 instead.

This subsystem holds the single definition rather than a copy of it: the view COALESCEs the newest resolution event over one legacy CASE, and the comment beside it records the divergence that motivated the view — one legacy row reading as accepted on one surface and as an active defect on another. Whether a given reader honours it is that reader's disposition, not this one's.

The schema makes a revision structurally mandatory on every claim and evidence row and refuses a validity interval that closes where it opened, and stops exactly where a substrate must: whether a recorded sha resolves, and whether it is an ancestor of the authority commit, needs git and is enforced in the claim handlers.

The generated and checked parties hold, but the schema carries hand-written prose about a vocabulary binding that the code has since falsified: the comment beside dispositions.evidence_quality states that a database created before the widening keeps the narrower constraint, and migrateVocabularyChecks rebuilds exactly that column on every open because the source declares the binding — a divergence in the one direction the four-party check does not look, since prose in schema.sql is not one of the four parties.

There is no resource here to have a lifecycle: schema.sql is text applied by B-02 at open, invariants.ts is pure predicates over a connection passed in, and the generated vocabulary module is frozen literals — the subsystem opens no handle, spawns no process, and writes no directory.

This subsystem is where the repository's own zero-denominator green is recorded and repaired: the schema names finding B03-2 in a comment and states the fix, which is that staleness lives on file_ledger because enforcePhasePrerequisites makes that table non-empty for any subsystem past scoping, so the denominator behind every derived staleness signal is non-empty by construction rather than by luck.

findings.symptom: schema.sql tells a reader of dispositions.evidence_quality that "databases created before this widening keep the narrower constraint", which stopped being true when the vocabulary CHECK migration landed: the source binds evidence_quality to that very column, so every open compares its live CHECK against the source and rebuilds the table when it is narrower.
findings.root_cause: The vocabulary contract has four parties and a check that compares them; hand-written prose inside schema.sql is a fifth, unchecked one. gen-vocabulary.mjs --check-sql compares CHECK literals, and check-evidence-vocabulary.mjs compares value lists, so neither reads a comment. When migrateVocabularyChecks was added in db.ts it made the statement obsolete and nothing in the repository could notice.
findings.business_context: Nothing computes differently because of it; the cost is to the next reader, and this file is the one a reader is most likely to trust, because it is where three of this repository's recorded defects are documented against themselves. Numbered B03-4 rather than B03-1: the ids B03-1 through B03-3 are cited by name in schema.sql's own comments for earlier defects, and reusing one in a rebuilt store would make those citations point at the wrong record.

claim_targets.challenge: adversarial probe for claim B-03/concurrency did not overturn it: every invariant helper takes the connection as an argument and is called inside the same synchronous handler as the write it authorizes, and the two that write do so inside db.transaction, so no in-process window exists between a prerequisite passing and the row it admitted.

adversarial probe for claim B-03/flow/status-advance/01 did not overturn it: enforcePhasePrerequisites checks the ledger count first and then requireStructuralClaim, and enforceForwardPrerequisites replays every intermediate rung, so an insert opening straight at a later status answers for the same evidence as an advance to it.

adversarial probe for claim B-03/key-type/mcp-server-contracts-conspectus-vocabulary-json-enums-evidence-kind did not overturn it: every value in the source carries label, meaning and cannot_justify, and the file-anchored rule in claims.ts admits exactly code-verified and contract-stated, so the enum states what a value withholds as well as what it grants.

adversarial probe for claim B-03/key-type/mcp-server-src-invariants-ts-enforcemonotonictransition did not overturn it: the guard returns early when either side is deferred, which is the bidirectional exemption the claim states, and throws only when the target rank is strictly lower — so an equal-rank rewrite passes and a regression does not.

The probe looked for a column other than valid_until_sha that a writer sets after insertion, and for a path that rewrites a statement in place; the claims_versions_are_immutable trigger aborts every such update, and no writer attempts one, so the close-plus-insert reading stands.

adversarial probe for claim B-03/state-container did not overturn it, with one qualification worth the record: the negative claim holds — nothing here is written after open — but "frozen set of literals" describes a compile-time guarantee. The generated arrays are `as const`, which is readonly to the type checker and an ordinary mutable array at run time; no code mutates them, so the claim's consequence stands while its word is stronger than the mechanism.

finding_verdicts.claim_b: adversarial probe for finding B03-4 did not find an overturning mechanism: gen-vocabulary.mjs --check-sql does read schema.sql, which is the one place a check could have noticed, but it extracts CHECK literals and compares value lists — it parses no comment. check-evidence-vocabulary.mjs reads SKILL.md's prose and not the schema's. dispositions.rationale: Every path this subsystem stores reaches requireWorkspaceSourcePath, directly or through the citation scanner, so an absolute path, a traversing one, or one pointing into reserved tool state is refused before it is written; and the scanner refuses the whole value on one bad token rather than keeping the good ones.

list_subsystems computes its confirmed_bugs rollup inline from the coarse findings.status column instead of joining finding_state_current, so the definition of "an open bug" is held here as well as in the view the schema says every reader of finding resolution selects from.

add_evidence takes ref_sha as an unvalidated string, so the row every disposition and finding cites can be bound to a revision that resolves in no repository; the claim and edge paths in this same subsystem both resolve their revisions against the bound workspace, which is what shows the omission to be an omission rather than a policy.

This subsystem consumes the generated vocabulary rather than restating it, and does so by filtering: the accepted file-anchored kinds are derived from EVIDENCE_KINDS, so dropping a kind from the source shrinks this rule with it instead of leaving it naming a kind nothing can carry. The citation grammar is exported as one pattern source and used for both the advertised schema and the handler's check.

These handlers open nothing and hold nothing: they read arguments, validate them, and write through the connection the context supplies, so the only resources with a lifecycle here are the short-lived git subprocesses the revision probes spawn and reap synchronously.

The strongest check here selects its subject by claim_key shape and returns silently for a key outside the pattern, which is the zero-denominator shape — but the exemption is stated in the contract rather than accidental, the pattern is anchored so it cannot be evaded by a prefix, and the categories it covers are exactly the ones a claim_key must use to record a type, container or flow at all.

findings.symptom: add_evidence writes an evidence row whose ref_sha was never resolved, so a disposition or finding can be published citing file:symbol@<sha> for a sha that names no commit in the bound workspace, and every reader downstream presents it as a revision binding.
findings.root_cause: The handler validates file_path through requireWorkspaceSourcePath and kind against the generated enum, then takes ref_sha with requireString and stores it. The module imports no git helper. Revision resolution in this server is attached to the citing record rather than to the cited row: add_claim resolves each evidence row's ref_sha and requires ancestry, and add_xref resolves every citation token, so evidence that only ever reaches a disposition or a finding is never resolved by anyone.
findings.business_context: The conspectus's central promise is that a reading is bound to a revision a later reader can check. The claim path keeps that promise and the evidence path does not, which is the worse of the two ways to be wrong: the surface that looks most like a citation is the one nothing verified. The repair is the probe this module does not have and seven others do — resolve ref_sha at write time and refuse the row — and it is cheap because add_evidence is already the single ingress for every evidence row.

findings.symptom: The confirmed_bugs rollup on every row list_subsystems returns is computed from findings.status, not from finding_state_current, so the dashboard's count of open bugs and a subsystem page's list of them are produced by two separate definitions of the same predicate.
findings.root_cause: finding_state_current was introduced because each reader had been mapping findings.status its own way, and its comment enumerates the readers that were converted: the renderer, the two findings tools, the review session, and the review historical-findings reader. list_subsystems was not among them and still carries a FILTER (WHERE f.status='confirmed-bug') in its LEFT JOIN.
findings.business_context: The two definitions agree at this revision because every transition tool writes the coarse column and the event in one transaction; verify_finding_fix already breaks that habit by writing only the event, so the agreement is a property of today's writers rather than of the model. The cost now is that the schema's stated invariant is false, and the next resolution state added will move the view and not this rollup.

claim_targets.challenge: adversarial probe for claim B-04/flow/record-an-edge/01 did not overturn it: add_xref's schema carries the citation pattern built from CITATION_TOKEN_SOURCE, the same exported string the handler's scanner compiles, so the advertised grammar and the enforced one cannot differ.

adversarial probe for claim B-04/flow/record-an-edge/02 did not overturn it: extractWorkspaceCitations throws on the first token whose revision does not resolve, before any citation is returned, so a value carrying one good token and one bad one is refused whole.

adversarial probe for claim B-04/flow/record-an-edge/03 did not overturn it, including the part most easily wrong: the comment does say "the eighth local copy of the two-line git probe", names findings.ts:37 and claims.ts:104, and states the reason they are not shared — each caller owns a different failure policy.

adversarial probe for claim B-04/key-type/mcp-server-src-tools-claims-ts-file-anchored-claim-key did not overturn it: the pattern is anchored at the start and matches only key-type, state-container and flow after the subsystem segment, so a key cannot slip the rule by prefixing it, and FILE_ANCHORED_EVIDENCE is a filter over the generated EVIDENCE_KINDS rather than a second literal list.

adversarial probe for claim B-04/key-type/mcp-server-src-tools-claims-ts-requirefileanchoredevidence did not overturn it: the predicate is a single rows.some over a conjunction, so two rows each satisfying one half cannot pass together, and the refusal string enumerates the kinds and paths it did find.

adversarial probe for claim B-04/state-container did not overturn it: the probe looked for module-level mutable state across every tool module in this subsystem — a cache, a memo, a lazily built index — and found only frozen constants and prepared statements built per call.

finding_verdicts.claim_b: adversarial probe for finding B04-4 did not find an overturning mechanism: the candidates were a downstream validator and the drift pass. detect_changes reconciles file_ledger.ref_sha and never reads evidence.ref_sha; standing's reachability check reads the ledger row, not the evidence row; and the only code that resolves an evidence row's revision is add_claim, which runs when a claim cites it and not when a disposition or finding does.

adversarial probe for finding B04-5 narrowed its scope. Claim A as Phase 3 implied it: the two definitions of "an open bug" can report different numbers. Claim B: they cannot at this revision, because add_finding and update_finding_status each write findings.status and the resolution event in one transaction, so status='confirmed-bug' and resolution_state='open' are equivalent today. In scope: the schema's stated invariant that every reader of finding resolution selects from the view, which is false, and the third copy of the predicate. Out of scope: any present disagreement between the dashboard count and a subsystem page. The finding stands as scope-restricted; verify_finding_fix already writes an event without touching the column, so the equivalence is a habit of today's writers and not a property of the model.

dispositions.rationale: Every path these tools store is guarded — fix_location through requireWorkspaceSourcePath and each primary_files entry through requireWorkspaceCitation — and the one unguarded string, a disposition's free-text evidence field, is never opened, joined on, or resolved: it is displayed, and non-strict parsing still refuses a value pointing into reserved tool state.

Both readers in this subsystem join finding_state_current and return its resolution_state beside the coarse column rather than instead of it, and the verification path reads finding_resolution_current directly, so nothing here holds a second mapping of findings.status.

set_disposition and add_finding both take ref_sha as an unvalidated string, and the disposition's free-text citation is parsed in non-strict mode, so a verdict can be bound to a revision that resolves nowhere; verify_finding_fix in the same module resolves both its revisions and checks ancestry, which shows the resolution is available and simply not applied where a reading is recorded.

This subsystem is where the drift the whole contract was built for was found — a tool accepting nine evidence qualities over a CHECK admitting five — and it now validates every enum argument against the generated arrays rather than a local list, so the tool side and the SQL side are two renderings of one source with parity asserted in CI.

Nothing here owns a resource: the durable state is an append-only table written through the connection B-02 holds, and the writes that must not interleave are wrapped in db.transaction rather than held under a handle of this subsystem's own.

The guards here cannot be satisfied by an absent subject: add_finding inserts the first resolution event in the same transaction as the finding, so no finding exists without a state to read, and the overturn guard requires evidence attached in the current session — a condition an empty evidence table fails rather than passes.

findings.symptom: A concern verdict and a confirmed bug are both stored with a ref_sha nobody resolved, so a disposition or finding can claim to have been assessed at a revision that exists in no repository, and every surface that prints the binding repeats the claim.
findings.root_cause: set_disposition and add_finding read ref_sha with requireString and write it. dispositions.ts imports no git helper at all; findings.ts has resolveCommit and applies it only to fix_sha, on the repair path. The disposition's free-text evidence citation is parsed with strict:false, which checks only that it does not point into reserved tool state before returning it verbatim, so the revision inside that string is unchecked too.
findings.business_context: The same omission as B04-4 at a different ingress, and the pair is what makes it a pattern rather than an oversight: revision resolution in this server is attached to the record that cites evidence, not to the record that states a reading. The repair path already shows the guard's shape — resolve both revisions, then ask whether one reaches the other — so the cost is one call per handler.

claim_targets.challenge: adversarial probe for claim B-05/concurrency did not overturn it: the probe looked for a read-modify-write over resolution state that two writers could interleave and found none — every transition reads the prior row only to build the event's rationale, and the insert does not depend on that read being still true.

adversarial probe for claim B-05/flow/read-a-findings-state/01 did not overturn it: both readers in findings.ts join finding_state_current and the verification path reads finding_resolution_current. The probe did find two readers outside this subsystem that do not — list_subsystems and the master-plan renderer — which is B04-5 and B08-1, not a counterexample to what this subsystem does.

adversarial probe for claim B-05/key-type/mcp-server-src-schema-sql-finding-state-current did not overturn it: the view LEFT JOINs finding_resolution_current, so every findings row appears exactly once and the CASE supplies a state for one that never received an event — the claim's "exactly one state" is a property of the join, not of the writers.

adversarial probe for claim B-05/state-container/mcp-server-src-tools-findings-ts-findingtools did not overturn it: no UPDATE or DELETE touches finding_resolution_events anywhere in the server or the materializer, add_finding inserts the finding and its first event in one transaction, and verify_finding_fix appends rather than amending — with a trigger refusing a verified-fixed event whose evidence is not attached as fix-verification.

finding_verdicts.claim_b: adversarial probe for finding B05-1 did not find an overturning mechanism: the schema is the other place a guard could live, and it constrains ref_sha to be present and non-empty on neither dispositions nor findings — both columns are plain nullable TEXT — so nothing below the handler asks whether the revision exists.

dispositions.rationale: The only agent-supplied argument here is a locus, which is matched against ledger and vocabulary rows and never opened, so there is no filesystem boundary to contain it against; the bound that does apply is enforced twice from one constant — advertised as maxLength and re-checked in code — so a host that validates its calls and one that does not are refused alike.

This is the subsystem the concern was written about and the one that honours it: every standing read selects from file_standing and every resolution read from finding_state_current, and the CASE expressions here aggregate over standing_state — a column the view already produced — rather than re-deriving it from classification and stale.

This subsystem reads revisions rather than recording them, and it is the one place where the record's meaning depends on ancestry and the check is made for that reason: a ledger row's examination revision is resolved and then asked whether it reaches HEAD, with an unresolvable revision and a resolvable one off this branch given different reasons rather than collapsed.

The reader surfaces import their labels and their cannot-justify lines from the generated module instead of restating them, and the enums they own carry no SQL binding, so those vocabularies have only the source and two generated copies as parties — both rewritten by the generator and compared by the checker.

These handlers are read-only and retain nothing between calls: each assembles an answer from views and tables and returns it, so there is no handle, no process, and no directory whose lifecycle could be wrong.

findings.root_cause: The files embed the separator and sentinel characters literally rather than as escapes: dev/test-rebuild-coverage.mjs uses a raw 0x00 in pairKey's join and in the batch-label comparison's default, and mcp-server/scripts/gen-vocabulary.mjs and dev/amanuensis-defects-to-pecia.mjs each carry two more. findings.business_context: Nothing computes differently: Node reads the byte as the code point the escape would have produced, so the run-time behaviour is identical. From the definer's side: both predicates are held once, as views the custodian's open asserts the existence of, and the reader on this seam consumes them without a fallback — the two copies that do exist are in B-04 and B-08, which are not parties here, and are recorded as B04-5 and B08-1.

seams.shared_object: finding_resolution_events and the current-state view over it
seams.notes: Assessed as SC-5 at 0fee11b, both sides confirmed-acceptable. Both parties treat the event spine as authority and the view as its single mapping: the appender writes one event per state change in the transaction that caused it, and the partitioner selects resolution_state from a view that LEFT JOINs one row per finding, so neither side can put a record in two partitions or in none. dispositions.rationale: From the appender's side: every state change is a row on finding_resolution_events written in the same transaction as the change that caused it, and this party's own readers go through the view rather than the column, so what it publishes to the partitioner is one state per finding with no second opinion behind it.

From the partitioner's side: the lens membership queries select resolution_state from the view, and because the view yields exactly one row per finding a record cannot satisfy two partitions or none by this party's own doing — a finding in both lenses or in neither would be a partition defect, which the projection's own state axis is what checks.

seams.shared_object: memory.db, opened read-only by the projection while the server holds it read-write
seams.notes: Assessed as SC-6 at 0fee11b, both sides confirmed-acceptable. The reader's connection is mode=ro, so it cannot repair the schema it finds and refuses the publish by name instead; the writer sets WAL, which is what permits the concurrent open, and truncate-checkpoints before any storage commit so the file a later reader sees carries every committed frame. Neither side claims a snapshot across a long publish, and the read-back compares finished bytes to a receipt precisely because there is none.

dispositions.rationale: From the reader's side: mode=ro is enforced at the connection, so this party cannot repair what it finds, and it does not try — an absent view refuses the publish by name instead of being created, which is what makes the probe a statement about the store rather than about the reader's willingness to leave it alone.

From the writer's side: WAL is what lets the reader open the same file without blocking, and the writer truncate-checkpoints before any storage commit, so the memory.db a later reader or a git checkout sees carries every committed frame; what neither side provides is a snapshot across a long publish, which both record rather than assume away.
